comparison: Perfect agreement on C1-C5. Both evaluations support the TCGA correlation and survival data as valid rationale for investigating Prdm1 function. OpenEval provides detailed statistical context while peer reviewers implicitly accept these bioinformatic findings without challenge.

Perfect agreement on C6-C7. Both evaluations support the conditional knockout model generation and validation. OpenEval notes standard experimental design with RT-PCR validation, while peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge the model adds specificity to experiments.

Strong agreement on C8-C13 (peer review covers C8-C10, C12-C13, omitting C11 which is background knowledge). Both evaluations support the impaired NK cell maturation findings across multiple tissues. OpenEval provides detailed flow cytometry analysis while peer reviewers acknowledge these as core phenotypic observations.

Perfect agreement on C14-C18. Both evaluations support the altered liver group 1 ILC subset findings. OpenEval notes quantitative changes with unclear mechanistic basis, while peer reviewers accept these as part of comprehensive characterization of Prdm1 function.

Perfect agreement on C19. Both evaluations support the negative in vivo cytotoxicity results. OpenEval notes this contrasts with other functional deficits, while peer reviewers accept it as consistent with mechanisms beyond direct cytotoxicity.

Perfect agreement on C20-C23. Both evaluations support the tumor metastasis and IFN-γ production findings. OpenEval notes the conclusion is strong given unaffected direct cytotoxicity, while peer reviewers explicitly recognize these as core findings demonstrating Prdm1's role in anti-tumor immunity.

Strong agreement on C24-C30 (bulk RNA-seq findings). OpenEval supports comprehensive transcriptional analysis with appropriate bioinformatics. Peer review R7 covers both bulk RNA-seq (C24-C30) and flow cytometry validation (C31-C34), accepting reduced cytotoxicity-related gene expression as a key contribution.

Agreement on C31-C34 (flow cytometry validation of RNA-seq). OpenEval supports the validation showing cytotoxic molecule reduction across maturation stages. Peer review R7 encompasses these findings as part of accepted transcriptional changes and their functional implications.

Perfect agreement on C35-C39. Both evaluations support the scRNA-seq experimental design, quality control, and clustering results. OpenEval notes consistency with flow cytometry data, while peer reviewers recognize the single-cell data as a valuable community resource.

Agreement on C40-C43 (Prf1 high cluster characterization). OpenEval supports the subclustering and functional enrichment analysis. Peer review R9 covers broader scRNA-seq findings (C40-C54) and accepts these as part of the study's characterization of Prdm1 regulation of JunB and NK cell maturation.

Agreement on C44-C50 (Junb high cluster characterization). OpenEval supports comprehensive characterization with reasonable inference about impaired anti-tumor activity, noting direct validation would strengthen conclusions. Peer review R9 accepts these findings as part of the Prdm1-JunB regulatory axis proposal.

Agreement on C51-C54 (Cxcr3 high cluster characterization). OpenEval supports the cluster characterization and ILC1 signature analysis. Peer review R9 encompasses these findings within the broader acceptance of scRNA-seq-based functional subset identification.

Agreement on C55-C62 (ILC1 subclustering). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to speculative plasticity claim (C62) requiring experimental validation. Peer review R10 supports the ILC1 characterization (covering C55-C61, C63, C65, C67-C68), accepting the findings as part of comprehensive approach while the speculation is presented cautiously.

Agreement on C63-C67 (Klra high cluster). OpenEval supports the characterization with reasonable but speculative functional interpretation. Peer review R10 covers these claims within broader ILC1 subset acceptance, consistent with the study's comprehensive characterization.
Agreement on C68-C69 (Gzmb high cluster). OpenEval supports the observation as consistent with overall phenotype. Peer review R10 includes C68 in accepted ILC1 characterization findings.

Strong agreement on C70-C74 (integrated analysis and Prdm1-Batf3 relationship). OpenEval supports the multi-dataset integration and negative regulation conclusion. Peer review R11 covers C70-C76, acknowledging the refined analysis compared to previous work and accepting shared regulatory targets.

Agreement on C75-C76 (comparison with Hobit knockout data). OpenEval supports the comparative analysis providing valuable context. Peer review R11 encompasses these findings, implicitly acknowledging the value of comparison with related transcription factor Hobit.

Divergence on C77-C83 (CellChat analysis). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting computational analysis appears sound though experimental validation would strengthen conclusions. Peer review R12 rates as UNCERTAIN, explicitly expressing concern about lack of experimental validation for in silico predictions, noting interesting findings remain unvalidated.

Perfect agreement on C84-C85. Both evaluations support the mitochondrial function findings. OpenEval notes interpretation about ATP synthesis may be premature without direct measurement. Peer reviewers accept findings as consistent with scRNA-seq data showing suppressed mitochondrial pathways.

Perfect agreement on C86-C87. Both evaluations support the tumor-bearing mice findings showing reduced cell numbers and impaired IFN-γ production. OpenEval notes consistency with overall phenotype, while peer reviewers accept these as supporting key conclusions about Prdm1's role in anti-tumor immunity.
OpenEval supports C88-C89 as appropriate definitional and background knowledge statements. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.

Divergence on C90-C91 (summary conclusions from scRNA-seq and CellChat). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting conclusions appropriately integrate multiple lines of evidence. Peer review R15 rates as UNCERTAIN, acknowledging scRNA-seq data quality but noting lack of mechanistic validation and that mechanistic conclusions about cellular communication require experimental validation beyond in silico analysis.
